newsitem.title: UK: Commodity markets take mixed view of Kremlin sacking.
newsitem.headline: Commodity markets take mixed view of Kremlin sacking.

text.p: The Kremlin power struggle which resulted in the sacking of Russia's security chief Alexander Leben on Thursday had a mixed impact on commodity prices.

Already-high crude oil prices jumped ahead and values for aluminium, of which Russia is also a big producer, turned from soggy to firm. But copper, lumbering under a huge stock overburden, ignored the news.

IPE Brent crude futures rallied on a combination of Russia and U.S. data showing oil stocks fell last week. December Brent crude futures were up 24 cents to $24.18 a barrel late but off the session high.
Russia is the third largest oil producer and a key supplier of crude to European markets.
Aluminium attracted some buying on the news. Russia exports over two million tonnes of aluminium a year to the West, roughly 10 percent of world supply.
"There is a chance that supplies could be disrupted if things get tricky," an analyst said.
Aluminium was indicated at $1,360, about $18 above the Wednesday close.
But palladium fixed at $115.75 per ounce, a fresh three-year low, despite Russia supply 66 percent of world needs.
The metal which is used in electronics, car emission catalysts and dentistry is caught between oversupply and low consumer demand. Gold was also unmoved, dealers said.

Copper, beset by worries about stocks overhanging the market, ignored Russia. The stock issue also took any buying interest out of confirmation a major U.S. copper refiner had gone on strike the prevous day, traders said.

Rumours of the strike at Kennecott's Utah smelter had caused a stir on Wednesday but confirmation of the partial shutdown -- management said some copper was still being produced at the 310,000 tonnes per year facility -- brought selling.
"It seemed to be the usual -- buy the rumour and sell the fact," one London Metal Exchange (LME) trader said.
The LME's flagship contract later edge up $9 to $1,924.
LIFFE wheat and barley futures closed lower with mixed reactions to the weekly European Union (EU) grain tender.
The EU granted licences for 332,500 tonnes of free market wheat at 6.90 ECU's.
"The result is encouraging but the restitutions could have been higher," said another.
Coffee futures came under pressure from origin sales to end mixed with November up $5 at $1,521, Jan down $10 at $1,424.
Cocoa and sugar were both flat with the former seeing some origin selling while sugar lacked fresh news to spur activity.
